edges.rationale: The Ethernet frame's source and destination address fields contain MAC addresses; understanding the frame format requires first knowing what link-layer addresses are and how they differ from IP addresses.
A switch's forwarding and filtering decisions are made by looking up destination MAC addresses, and self-learning records source MAC addresses; MAC addressing is a direct prerequisite.
Switches operate on Ethernet frames, parsing the destination address field to forward/filter and the source address field to learn; the frame structure must be understood first.

The advantages attributed to switches (collision elimination via per-interface bandwidth, full-duplex operation, transparent plug-and-play administration) only make sense once the switch's forwarding and self-learning mechanics are understood.
Appreciating how switches eliminate collisions requires knowing that classic Ethernet evolved from a shared broadcast medium where hubs and collisions were inherent.

The comparison centers on how switches forward frames using MAC addresses and self-learning versus how routers forward datagrams; switch operation must be understood before contrasting it with routing.
The switch-vs-router trade-off hinges on layer-2 MAC-address forwarding versus layer-3 IP-address forwarding, which presupposes knowledge of both addressing schemes.
VLANs partition a single physical switch into isolated virtual switches; understanding per-VLAN forwarding, filtering, and learning requires the base switch operation first.
VLAN membership and traffic isolation are carried in the Ethernet frame itself (e.g., 802.1Q VLAN tag inserted into the frame), so the frame format is needed to understand the mechanism.
